title: Marijuana Prohibition, Wasted Police Resources and Finite Justice

content_html_sanitized:
When I wrote about the 30 million marijuana arrests in America over the last 50 years, I focused primarily on the injustice and the human consequences.

See Long-Term Mental Health Consequences of Being Arrested on Arrestees and Their Families


However, there are other less obvious costs, and they may mean different things from different perspectives.


First, all of the components of the criminal justice system have finite resources. The police departments, from the smallest towns to the biggest cities, have a limited number of officers. Within these departments there are a limited number of patrolmen, detectives, etc. The same is true at the Federal level.


For example, for supporters of the broader Drug War these thirty million marijuana arrests, bookings, prosecutions, plea bargaining,  sentencing, probation supervision, drug testing, etc. all used resources that could have been used in the efforts to suppress the trade in heroin, or crack, or methamphetamine, or fentanyl, etc.


The fact that most of these cases end in probation and little or no jail time, does not reduce the burden on these finite resources. And what about investigating rape cases? Or murders? Or armed robberies? Or terrorism?


From almost twenty five years ago, less than nine months before the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center, see

Marijuana Arrests In New York City Continue to Soar. Arrests Will Exceed 60,000 for this Year. Up From Only 720 in 1992!


Or maybe it’s even worse? 

See  Did The Drug War Claim Another 3,056 Casualties On 9-11? Ariana Huffington’s Extraordinary Indictment.
